As Zhongfeng said, 'Chan is the Chan of Pure Land, Pure Land is the Pure Land of Chan; those who practise must value going deep through one gate.' Mahāsthāmaprāpta entered the acceptance of non-arising through recollecting the Buddha; Samantabhadra vowed to be born in Sukhāvatī.
speaker: Yunqi Zhuhong

original.text: 且汝既了徹自心，隨處淨土。吾試問汝：『還肯即廁溷中作住止否？……』於斯數者，歡喜安隱，略不介意，許汝說高山平地總西方。
original.edition: Taishō T47n1977 (CBETA XML P5, local copy sources_raw/cbeta), 420b05-11
original.licence: CBETA CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 (text quoted for reference)

paraphrase: If 'the pure mind is the Pure Land, so there is no seven-jewelled world', then by the same token there would be no heavens and no hells. True understanding of principle knows there is no principle outside phenomena; the lands are of four kinds, not only the land of eternal quiescent light. If you have truly seen through your own mind so that every place is the Pure Land — would you live in a latrine, eat from the trough with dogs and pigs, sleep among rotting corpses, nurse lepers for months? If you can do so with joy and without a thought, I grant that you may say 'high mountains and flat ground are all the West'; otherwise pure and impure are not yet empty for you, and to deny the buddha-land is to deceive heaven and men.
speaker: Yunqi Zhuhong

original.text: 此淨土法門似淺而深，似近而遠，似難而易，似易而難，他日汝當自知。汝今參禪、念佛，不妨隨便一門深入。
original.edition: Taishō T47n1977 (CBETA XML P5, local copy sources_raw/cbeta), 420b22-24
original.licence: CBETA CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 (text quoted for reference)

paraphrase: If you have the strength and vow to go in and out of the sea of birth-and-death doing the bodhisattva work without fear, I will not press the Pure Land on you; but if you fear the strong winds of this world, the rarity of buddhas, the weakness of your acceptance, that you may not end birth-and-death in this body and that the road after death is dark — then to reject the Pure Land is no small loss. This teaching seems shallow but is deep, near but far, hard but easy, easy but hard; whether you practise Chan or recollection, go deep through one gate, but do not mistake brass for gold and slander the Pure Land.
speaker: Yunqi Zhuhong

location.section: commentary on 'holding fast to the name' (執持名號)

paraphrase: Holding the name is of two kinds: holding it in phenomena (shichi) — hearing of the Buddha and reciting his name continuously, remembering and not forgetting, with faith but without yet penetrating principle; and holding it in principle (lichi) — seeing that the reciting mind and the Buddha recited are not two. Each matures into the undistracted single mind in its phenomenal and principled forms.
speaker: Yunqi Zhuhong
notes: Not read locally; recalled.

location.section: commentary on the Smaller Sūtra's exhortation to aspire

paraphrase: Faith, vow and holding the name are the three provisions for birth, like the three legs of a tripod. Whether one is born depends entirely on having faith and vow; the height of one's grade depends entirely on the depth of holding the name. Faith is to believe in oneself, in others, in cause, in effect, in phenomena and in principle; vow is to loathe this Sahā world and delight in the Land of Bliss.
speaker: Ouyi Zhixu
notes: T37 not local; wording recalled, no original.

original.text: 《華嚴經》云「信為道元功德母，長養一切諸善根。」然世之所謂修淨土者，不可以不信也。
original.edition: Taishō T47n1970 (CBETA XML P5, local copy sources_raw/cbeta), 251a05-06
original.licence: CBETA CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 (text quoted for reference)

paraphrase: 'Faith is the source of the way and the mother of merit, nourishing all good roots' (Avataṃsaka): those who practise the Pure Land cannot be without faith; the Western land and its adornments are described in the Amitābha Sūtra, and Amitābha before becoming a buddha made forty-eight vows, each to save people.
speaker: Wang Rixiu

location.section: essay on the three great essentials at the end of life (臨終三大要)

paraphrase: Three essentials for the dying: first, skilfully instruct and comfort the dying person so that right faith arises; second, let family and friends recite the Buddha's name in shifts to support the dying one's pure recollection; third, strictly avoid moving the body or weeping, lest the dying one be disturbed and lose right mindfulness.
speaker: Yinguang
notes: Recalled; exact title and wording not checked (recent).

paraphrase: Fulfil your human relations and duties, guard against evil and keep sincerity, do no evil and practise all good; truly for the sake of birth-and-death arouse the aspiration for awakening, and with deep faith and vow hold the Buddha's name.
speaker: Yinguang
notes: Recalled formula; wording not checked (recent).

paraphrase: The teaching and practice for birth in the Land of Bliss are the eyes and feet for this defiled world in its last age; monks and lay, high and low, all should turn to it. The exoteric and esoteric teachings and the practices of principle and phenomena are many; for the wise and diligent they are not hard, but for a dull person like me they are difficult; therefore I have gathered passages on the single gate of the nenbutsu from the sūtras and treatises, so that they are easy to understand and practise.
speaker: Genshin
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

location.section: great chapter 1: loathing and leaving the defiled realm (厭離穢土)

paraphrase: The first chapter describes the six paths to be loathed — the eight great hells with their torments in detail, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans and gods — showing the human body as impure, suffering and impermanent and even heavenly life as ending in the five signs of decay, so that the practitioner will turn away from the three realms.
speaker: Genshin
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

location.section: great chapter 2: joyfully seeking the Pure Land (欣求淨土)

paraphrase: The second chapter sets out ten pleasures of the Pure Land: being welcomed by the holy assembly at death, the first opening of the lotus, the pleasure of the body and superknowledges, of the wondrous objects, of unending joy, of guiding one's connections, of the holy company, of seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, of making offerings to the buddhas at will, and of advancing on the Buddha-path.
speaker: Genshin
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. List of the ten pleasures recalled (moderate).

location.section: great chapter 4: the right practice of the nenbutsu (正修念佛)

paraphrase: The right practice follows Vasubandhu's five gates — worship, praise, aspiration, contemplation and transfer — with contemplation at the centre: the particular contemplation of the Buddha's marks one by one, the general contemplation of his whole body, and the abbreviated contemplation for those who cannot manage these — contemplating the light of the white tuft between his brows, or simply thinking 'I too am within his embrace; though passions blind my eyes and I cannot see him, his great compassion never tires and always shines upon me'; and for those unable even to contemplate, single-mindedly calling the name.
speaker: Genshin
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Shinran cites the 'I too am within his embrace' passage in the Shōshinge.

location.section: great chapter 6: nenbutsu at special times — deathbed practice (臨終行儀)

paraphrase: Deathbed practice: following the Jetavana custom the sick monk is moved to a separate hall of impermanence; an image of Amitābha is placed facing west with a five-coloured cord tied to its hand, the other end held by the dying; attendants burn incense, scatter flowers and keep the dying person's mind on the Buddha; they ask what he sees and help him repent evil signs; the dying one should call the name, and at the last moments the attendants help him complete ten recitations in right mindfulness. Genshin also gives exhortations for the attendant to speak at the bedside.
speaker: Genshin
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Cf. the Nijūgo zanmai-e rules.

paraphrase: For the act that leads to birth, the nenbutsu is the foundation.
speaker: Genshin
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. The phrase 往生之業念佛為本 is widely quoted as Genshin's (e.g. by Hōnen); chapter location not verified.

paraphrase: Kūya always recited Amida's name, so people called him 'Amida hijiri'; he travelled everywhere, dug wells where water was lacking and built bridges; before his time few in the capital practised the nenbutsu, after him all did; at his death he faced west and passed away amid fragrance and music.
speaker: Yoshishige no Yasutane
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Content of the entry recalled in outline (low).

paraphrase: Following Daochuo, all the Buddha's teachings fall into two gates, the holy path and the Pure Land; one should set aside the holy path and take refuge in the Pure Land. The Pure Land school has its canon — the three sūtras (the Larger, the Contemplation and the Amitābha) and one treatise (Vasubandhu's) — and its lineages of transmission (Hōnen names those of Huiyuan, of Cimin and of Daochuo–Shandao).
speaker: Hōnen
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: Following Shandao, set aside the miscellaneous practices and take the right: the five right practices, of which calling the name is the rightly determined act and the others auxiliary. Right and miscellaneous differ in five pairs: intimate or distant, near or far, uninterrupted or interrupted, not requiring transfer or requiring transfer of merit, pure or mixed.
speaker: Hōnen
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: Dharmākara, surveying 21 billion buddha-lands, selected (senchaku) the good and rejected the bad; in the eighteenth vow he rejected all other practices and selected solely the nenbutsu as the practice for birth. Why? First, superior and inferior: the name contains all the virtues of the Buddha's inner realization and outer activity, as the word 'house' contains beams, rafters and pillars, whereas other practices each hold only a part. Second, difficult and easy: the nenbutsu is easy for all; if building images and stūpas were the vow's practice the poor would lose hope, if wisdom the dull, if much learning the little-learned, if keeping precepts the precept-breakers — who are the many; so, out of compassion for all equally, he chose the nenbutsu alone.
speaker: Hōnen
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: The Larger Sūtra mentions other practices for the three grades besides the nenbutsu; this may be read in three ways — they are taught in order to be abandoned in favour of the nenbutsu (establishing by abandoning), as aids to the nenbutsu, or as secondary parallel paths; Hōnen takes the first as the main intent, the Buddha's aim being exclusive nenbutsu.
speaker: Hōnen
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: The practitioner of the nenbutsu must possess the three minds of the Contemplation Sūtra, sincere, deep and aspiring; quoting Shandao at length, Hōnen explains that the deep mind includes deep entrusting that one is an ordinary being of sin and that one will surely be born by the vow; those lacking the three minds are not born.
speaker: Hōnen
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

location.section: ch. 16, conclusion: the passage of the threefold selection

paraphrase: If you wish quickly to leave birth-and-death, of the two excellent teachings set aside the holy path and choose to enter the Pure Land; wishing to enter the Pure Land, of the right and miscellaneous practices cast aside the miscellaneous and choose to take refuge in the right; wishing to practise the right, of the rightly determined and auxiliary acts set aside the auxiliary and choose the rightly determined. The rightly determined act is to call the Buddha's name; calling the name, one will surely be born, because it is based on the Buddha's primal vow.
speaker: Hōnen
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: Hōnen explains that he relies solely on Shandao, whose commentary is like a sūtra, as the 'master' of the Pure Land; he wrote the work at the request of the regent (Kanezane) and asks that, once read, it be buried in the wall and not left by the window, lest those who slander the Dharma see it and fall into evil paths.
speaker: Hōnen
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: The nenbutsu I teach is not the contemplation of the Buddha discussed by the learned of China and Japan, nor the recitation that comes from studying and understanding its meaning; it is only to say 'Namu Amida Butsu' without doubt that one will be born, and so to be born. The three minds and four modes are all contained in the conviction that one will be born by saying Namu Amida Butsu. If I held some deeper teaching besides this, I would lose the compassion of Śākyamuni and Amida and fall out of the vow. Those who believe in the nenbutsu, even if they have thoroughly learned all the teachings of Śākyamuni's lifetime, should behave as ignorant people who know not a single letter, as unlettered nuns and lay-folk, and without showing learning just say the nenbutsu single-heartedly.
speaker: Hōnen
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: Hōnen's disciples pledge: not to attack the Tendai and Shingon teachings or slander other buddhas and bodhisattvas; not to engage the learned or other practitioners in disputes; not to tell those of other practices to abandon them, or mock them; not to say that the nenbutsu has no precepts, encouraging lust, wine and meat, or that one who keeps precepts is a practitioner of miscellaneous practice and that relying on the vow one need not fear evil; not to spread their own ideas as the master's teaching; not to preach wrong doctrines to the ignorant; not to teach heresies in the master's name.
speaker: Hōnen
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Article wording paraphrased from memory; order not verified.

paraphrase: Take it in faith that birth is attained by a single calling, yet in practice strive all your life; to doubt that one calling suffices is to doubt the Buddha's vow, and to neglect continued calling because one suffices is also wrong — believe with the one calling, practise with the whole life.
speaker: Hōnen
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Gist recalled from several letters; exact source letter not identified.

paraphrase: Live your present life in whatever way lets you best say the nenbutsu; whatever hinders the nenbutsu, give it up. If you cannot say it as a wandering hijiri, say it married; if you cannot say it married, say it as a hijiri; if living alone hinders it, live with others; food, clothing and shelter are aids to the nenbutsu.
speaker: Hōnen
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: Having read the whole canon several times without finding a way for someone like himself who could keep neither precepts nor meditation nor wisdom, Hōnen in 1175 came upon Shandao's line 'single-heartedly and exclusively recollecting the name of Amida ... this is the rightly determined act, because it accords with that Buddha's vow', and at once abandoned all other practices for the nenbutsu.
speaker: narrator
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Scroll number not verified.

paraphrase: At Ōhara, before Tendai and Nara scholars, Hōnen explained that the holy path suits those of superior capacity while the Pure Land path is for ordinary people of this age, and that his own capacity was too poor for the former; the listeners were moved and joined in the nenbutsu for days.
speaker: narrator
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Participants and details recalled only in outline.

paraphrase: The universal vow difficult to fathom is a great ship bearing us across the sea hard to cross; the unhindered light is the sun of wisdom dispelling the darkness of ignorance. When the occasion for the Pure Land teaching had matured, Devadatta led Ajātaśatru to harm, and Śākyamuni led Vaidehī to choose the Land of Peace; the auspicious name that embodies all virtues and the true shinjin are the way for those of the last age. How joyful I am, Gutoku Shinran, to have met the teaching of India, China and Japan.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: There are two aspects of Amida's transfer of merit, going and returning; in the going aspect there are true teaching, practice, shinjin and realization. The true teaching is the Larger Sūtra of Immeasurable Life: its essential purport is Amida's primal vow and its substance is the name; the Buddha appeared in the world precisely to reveal it.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: The great practice is to say the name of the Tathāgata of Unhindered Light; it contains all good and all roots of virtue and comes from the vow that all buddhas praise the name (seventeenth); it is not a practice the ordinary being performs and transfers by self-power but one transferred by Amida (non-transferring practice); calling the name breaks the ignorance of beings and fulfils their aspirations.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: Great shinjin is the true cause of birth; it is hard to attain, not because the practice is difficult but because shinjin is difficult. The three minds of the eighteenth vow — sincere mind, entrusting and aspiration for birth — are all Amida's true mind given to beings and are one mind, the single mind of Vasubandhu; there is no true mind in the foolish being. Shinjin arises in 'one thought-moment', the ultimate brevity of time, when the person enters the rightly established state; this is crosswise transcendence.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: One who attains the diamond-like true mind gains ten benefits in the present life: protection by unseen beings, possession of supreme virtue, turning of evil into good, protection by all buddhas, praise by all buddhas, constant protection by the Buddha's light, much joy of heart, awareness of the Buddha's benevolence and its repayment, constant practice of great compassion, and entry into the rightly established state.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. List recalled.

location.section: chapter on Shinjin, the 'difficult to cure'

paraphrase: Quoting the Nirvāṇa Sūtra at length, Shinran shows that those difficult to cure — those who slander the Dharma, commit the grave offences, or lack the seed of buddhahood — are healed by the Buddha's compassion, as Ajātaśatru, who killed his father, was freed of his remorse and illness on meeting the Buddha and awakened 'rootless faith'.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: True realization is the wondrous fruit of perfect benefit for others, from the vow of necessary attainment of nirvāṇa (eleventh): the ordinary being full of passions who attains the shinjin of the going aspect joins the rightly established group in this life and necessarily reaches nirvāṇa, which is eternal bliss, dharma-body, suchness, one-thusness; from suchness appear the bodies of the Buddha. The returning aspect (twenty-second vow) is the benefit of teaching others after birth.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

location.section: chapter on the True Buddha and Land

paraphrase: The true Buddha is the Tathāgata of inconceivable light and the true land is the land of immeasurable light, established by the vows of light and life (twelfth and thirteenth); both are the reward of the vow; there are true and provisional (transformed) buddhas and lands.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

location.section: chapter on the Transformed Buddhas and Lands

paraphrase: Those who practise various goods (nineteenth vow) or say the name by self-power (twentieth) are born in the transformed land — the borderland, the womb-palace, the realm of indolence and pride. Shinran confesses that, following the treatise-master and the master's guidance, he left the provisional gate of the myriad practices and good acts, turned to the true gate of the self-power nenbutsu, and then left it to enter the ocean of the selected vow, the eighteenth.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

location.section: chapter on the Transformed Buddhas and Lands

paraphrase: The teachings of the holy path are suited to the time when the Buddha was in the world and to the right Dharma age, not to the semblance and last ages; reckoning the years since the Buddha's passing, Shinran finds the present in the last age, and quotes the Lamp for the Last Age: in the last age there are only monks in name, who are nonetheless to be honoured.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Shinran's year-count omitted (not recalled with certainty).

location.section: end of the chapter on Transformed Lands

paraphrase: Quoting sūtras, Shinran teaches that one who has taken refuge in the Buddha should not take refuge in other gods and spirits, nor observe auspicious days and divination; non-Buddhist teachings are to be distinguished from the true.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Content recalled in outline.

paraphrase: The monks of the holy path in the temples, blind to the teaching, and the scholars of the capital, confused about true and false, together with the ruler and ministers, acting against the Dharma, punished the master Hōnen and his disciples without trial — some were executed, others defrocked and exiled; Shinran was one. Therefore he is now neither monk nor layman and has taken 'Toku' (bald-head) as his surname. In 1201 he abandoned the miscellaneous practices and took refuge in the primal vow; in 1205 he was permitted to copy the Senchakushū and the master's portrait. He writes with joy and gratitude at having met the teaching.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

location.section: lines 1-2 and the passage on the vow

paraphrase: I take refuge in the Tathāgata of Immeasurable Life, I entrust myself to the Buddha of Inconceivable Light. ... The name of the primal vow is the act of right assurance; the vow of sincere mind and entrusting is the cause; to attain equal enlightenment and realise great nirvāṇa is fulfilled by the vow of necessary attainment of nirvāṇa.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: When ordinary beings, good or evil, hear and entrust themselves to the Tathāgata's universal vow, the Buddha praises them as persons of vast and excellent understanding and calls them white lotuses; yet for evil beings of wrong views and arrogance, to accept and hold the nenbutsu of Amida's primal vow with joyful trust is the most difficult of difficulties.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: The masters of India, China and Japan revealed the Buddha's intent: Nāgārjuna taught the easy practice and that one who recollects Amida's vow at once enters the stage of assurance; Vasubandhu took refuge with single mind; Tanluan made other-power plain; Daochuo showed that the holy path is hard to realise and only the Pure Land passable; Shandao revealed the Buddha's true intent and the deep entrusting; Genshin said that though passions blind our eyes, great compassion constantly illumines us; Hōnen showed that doubt keeps us in birth-and-death and that shinjin is the entrance to nirvāṇa.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: Those who rejoice in shinjin are said to be equal to the Tathāgatas; great shinjin is buddha-nature, buddha-nature is the Tathāgata.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

location.section: hymns on benefits in the present life

paraphrase: When one says Namu Amida Butsu, the benefits in this present life are boundless: evil karma of transmigration is removed, untimely death is averted, the gods of heaven and earth and the guardian kings protect the person day and night, the demons are afraid.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Recalled in outline.

paraphrase: Hymns praising Nāgārjuna, Vasubandhu, Tanluan, Daochuo, Shandao, Genshin and Hōnen, the last called the manifestation of Amida (or of Seishi) who appeared to spread the teaching of the selected primal vow in Japan.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: More than two thousand years have passed since Śākyamuni entered nirvāṇa; the true and semblance ages are over — disciples of the last age, lament! In the last age of five turbidities beings cannot practise and realise; the teachings the Buddha left have all gone to the Dragon Palace; but Amida's universal vow remains.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: Although I have taken refuge in the true Pure Land teaching, a true and sincere mind is hard to have; I am false and untrue, without the least pure mind. Outwardly each of us shows wisdom, goodness and diligence; inwardly greed, anger, wrongdoing and deceit abound, like a serpent or scorpion.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: The Buddha's coming to welcome at death belongs to those who seek birth by various practices, being practitioners of self-power; waiting for the moment of death and relying on the welcoming apply to them. The person of true shinjin, because he is embraced and never abandoned, dwells in the rightly established state; his birth is settled when shinjin is settled; he need not wait for the moment of death or rely on being welcomed.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

location.section: letter on jinen hōni (自然法爾章)

paraphrase: 'Ji' means 'of itself', not through the practitioner's calculation; 'nen' means 'to be made so', by the Tathāgata's vow; 'hōni' means being so by virtue of the Dharma, the working of the vow. Since the practitioner does not calculate, 'no working is true working'. The vow is to make us become the supreme Buddha; the supreme Buddha is formless, and because formless is called jinen; Amida Buddha is the means by which we are made to know jinen. Having understood this, one should not keep discussing jinen, lest 'no working' become again a working.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Letter numbering as commonly given (moderate).

paraphrase: Because there is medicine, do not delight in poison: some say that since the vow saves evil people one may do evil as one pleases; this is utterly wrong — as one hears the teaching and entrusts oneself, one comes to reject evil, and those who deliberately do what should not be done in the name of the vow harm the community and the teacher.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. The saying appears in Shinran's letters and is echoed in Tannishō 13; exact letter not pinned down.

location.section: letters on the person of shinjin

paraphrase: The person of true shinjin, being certain to attain supreme awakening, is 'the same as Maitreya' and 'equal to the Tathāgatas' — though the body is that of a foolish being, the heart is already equal to the Tathāgatas.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: One should not insist on 'one-calling' or 'many-calling' as the true teaching; the nenbutsu of the primal vow includes both, and to set one against the other goes against the teaching. 'Immediately attaining birth' means that at the moment shinjin arises one dwells in non-retrogression, without waiting for another time or another day.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: Buddha-nature is dharma-nature, dharma-body; this Tathāgata pervades the countless worlds — the hearts of the ocean of all beings; it is said that plants, trees and land all attain buddhahood. Because this heart of all beings entrusts itself to the vow of the dharma-body, that shinjin is buddha-nature. From this formless dharma-body appeared the form called Dharmākara, who made the vows and became Amida of Unhindered Light.
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Gist recalled; exact wording not checked.

paraphrase: The teachings divide into two pairs and four levels: vertical and crosswise, going out and transcending. Vertical transcendence is the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna (becoming a buddha in this body); vertical going out is the gradual teaching of the Mahāyāna (and of the two vehicles); crosswise going out is the Pure Land teaching of various practices and self-power nenbutsu (nineteenth and twentieth vows); crosswise transcendence is the other-power shinjin of the primal vow (eighteenth).
speaker: Shinran
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: When, entrusting ourselves to the inconceivable working of Amida's vow and believing we will be born, the thought of saying the nenbutsu arises within, we are at that moment brought to share in the benefit of being embraced, never to be abandoned. Amida's vow does not discriminate between young and old, good and evil; only shinjin is essential, for the vow is to save beings heavy with evil and ablaze with passions. So no other good is needed, for no good surpasses the nenbutsu, and no evil need be feared, for no evil obstructs Amida's vow.
speaker: Shinran (as recorded)
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Tannishō section numbering standard.

paraphrase: To followers who had come from the Kantō at the risk of their lives to ask about the way to birth: 'As for me, Shinran, there is nothing but to receive and entrust myself to the teaching of my master that we are saved by Amida simply by saying the nenbutsu. Whether the nenbutsu is the seed of birth in the Pure Land or the act that will send me to hell, I do not know. Even if deceived by Hōnen I would have no regret, for I am incapable of any other practice and hell is my dwelling anyway. If Amida's vow is true, Śākyamuni's teaching cannot be false ... Beyond this, whether you take up the nenbutsu or abandon it is for each of you to decide.'
speaker: Shinran (as recorded)
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Tannishō section numbering standard.

paraphrase: Even a good person attains birth in the Pure Land, how much more an evil person. People commonly say the reverse, but that goes against the intent of the other-power vow: those who do good by self-power, lacking the mind of total reliance on other-power, are not the object of Amida's vow; when they turn from self-power and entrust themselves to other-power they attain the true land. Amida made the vow out of pity for us who, full of passions, cannot free ourselves by any practice; its intent is the evil person's attaining buddhahood, so the evil person who entrusts himself to other-power is the true object (shōki) of birth.
speaker: Shinran (as recorded)
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Tannishō section numbering standard.

paraphrase: Compassion differs between the path of sages and the Pure Land path: the former is to pity, sympathise with and care for beings, but one can hardly save them as one wishes; the latter is quickly to become a buddha by the nenbutsu and with great compassion benefit beings as one wishes. In this life, however much we pity others, we cannot fully save them; only the nenbutsu is the thoroughgoing compassion.
speaker: Shinran (as recorded)
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Tannishō section numbering standard.

paraphrase: Shinran has never said the nenbutsu even once as a memorial service for his father and mother, for all beings have been parents and siblings through many lives; the nenbutsu is not a good one does and transfers by one's own power; only after becoming a buddha can one save them.
speaker: Shinran (as recorded)
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Tannishō section numbering standard.

paraphrase: It is absurd for followers of the exclusive nenbutsu to quarrel over 'my disciples' and 'others' disciples'; Shinran does not have a single disciple, for people say the nenbutsu through Amida's working, not his; we meet and part according to conditions.
speaker: Shinran (as recorded)
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Tannishō section numbering standard.

paraphrase: The nenbutsu is the single path free of hindrance: the gods of heaven and earth bow before the practitioner of shinjin, the demons and non-Buddhists cannot obstruct him, his karmic evil cannot bear fruit, and no good acts equal it.
speaker: Shinran (as recorded)
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Tannishō section numbering standard.

paraphrase: For the practitioner the nenbutsu is neither a practice nor a good act: it is not practice because it is not done by one's own designs, not good because it is not produced by one's own designs; being wholly other-power and free of self-power, it is neither practice nor good.
speaker: Shinran (as recorded)
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Tannishō section numbering standard.

paraphrase: Yuien asks why, though he says the nenbutsu, he feels no dancing joy nor any wish to go quickly to the Pure Land. Shinran answers that he has the same doubt; that we do not rejoice at what should make us dance with joy is the working of blind passions — and the Buddha, knowing this, made the vow for such foolish beings, so we can be all the more sure. We cling to this old home of suffering and do not long for the Pure Land; when our karmic bond with this world is exhausted and we die, we will go there; the Buddha pities especially those without longing to go quickly.
speaker: Shinran (as recorded)
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Tannishō section numbering standard.

paraphrase: In the nenbutsu, no working (no calculation) is true working, for it is beyond words, description and conception.
speaker: Shinran (as recorded)
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Tannishō section numbering standard.

paraphrase: Asked whether he would do whatever Shinran said, Yuien agreed; told to kill a thousand people to be sure of birth, he said he could not kill even one. Shinran: then you see that it is not by a good mind that one does not kill, nor by an evil mind that one kills — if karmic conditions so arise, one might kill a hundred or a thousand. To fear doing evil and think that thereby one is fit or unfit for the vow is not to entrust oneself to it; yet Shinran also rebuked those who boasted of doing evil because the vow saves the evil ('do not take poison because there is an antidote').
speaker: Shinran (as recorded)
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Tannishō section numbering standard.

paraphrase: The compiler laments the view that one attains awakening in this very body while still full of passions: that is the teaching of the Shingon and Lotus schools, attainable by few; in the Pure Land teaching one entrusts oneself to the vow in this life and attains awakening in the Pure Land.
speaker: compiler / Rennyo
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Tannishō section numbering standard.

paraphrase: Shinran often said: when I consider deeply the vow Amida pondered for five kalpas, it was for me, Shinran, alone; how grateful I am for the vow that resolved to save me, burdened with so much karma. ... I know nothing of what is good or evil; for the foolish being full of passions in this burning house of an impermanent world, all things are empty and false, without any truth; only the nenbutsu is true.
speaker: Shinran (as recorded)
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Tannishō section numbering standard.

paraphrase: Rennyo's colophon: this is an important text of our school, not to be shown indiscriminately to those lacking the karmic roots from the past.
speaker: compiler / Rennyo
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Tannishō section numbering standard.

paraphrase: Eshinni writes that Shinran left Mt Hiei, secluded himself at the Rokkakudō for a hundred days praying about the life to come, and at dawn of the ninety-fifth day received a verse from Prince Shōtoku; he then went to Hōnen for a hundred days, rain or shine, and heard that for good and evil people alike the way of release is simply to say the nenbutsu; and that Shinran used to say he would go wherever Hōnen went, even to hell.
speaker: Eshinni
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: In the dream at the Rokkakudō (1201) the bodhisattva Kannon (Guze Kannon, as Prince Shōtoku) said to Shinran: 'If the practitioner, by past karma, should be bound to a woman, I will take the form of a woman and be embraced; throughout life I will adorn his life and at death lead him to the Land of Bliss.'
speaker: Kannon (in the dream, as reported by Kakunyo)
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Content recalled; also preserved in Takada documents.

paraphrase: When we consider the fleeting nature of human life, it is like an illusion from beginning to end; in the morning we may have rosy cheeks, in the evening be white ashes; when the winds of impermanence blow, eyes close, breath stops, the face loses its colour; family and relatives weep, but nothing can be done; the body is cremated and only white ashes remain. So everyone should take to heart the one great matter of the life to come, rely deeply on Amida Buddha, and say the nenbutsu.
speaker: Rennyo
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: Lay men and women of this last age, ignorant of the teaching, should abandon all miscellaneous practices and single-heartedly and deeply rely on Amida, asking him to save them in the life to come; then, without doubt, they will be saved; after that, say the nenbutsu in gratitude for as long as you live.
speaker: Rennyo
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: Keep the laws of the land as fundamental (ōbō ihon) and humanity and justice first; do not disparage other buddhas, bodhisattvas and kami, for they are included in Amida; do not speak of the teaching indiscriminately in public; keep shinjin deep within.
speaker: Rennyo
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Composite of several letters.

paraphrase: Rennyo rejects the view that birth was already settled ten kalpas ago when Amida attained buddhahood so that no entrusting is now needed (jikkō anjin), the secret teachings transmitted in private (hiji bōmon), and the view that simply saying the name without shinjin brings birth; what is required is to rely on Amida single-heartedly.
speaker: Rennyo
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Composite; letters not individually identified.

paraphrase: Amida's attainment of perfect awakening and our birth were accomplished at the same time; in Namu Amida Butsu the person (ki) who entrusts and the Dharma (hō) that saves are one; the Buddha's body itself is our practice, so the practitioner does nothing of his own.
speaker: (anonymous)
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted.

paraphrase: After a monk refused the talisman saying he had no faith, Ippen prayed at the Kumano Hongū; the deity (the avatar of Amida) appeared and said: 'Holy man spreading the nenbutsu, why do you spread it mistakenly? It is not by your recommending that beings come to be born; the birth of all beings in the ten directions was settled as Namu Amida Butsu at Amida's perfect awakening ten kalpas ago. Distribute the talismans without choosing between those with and without faith, and without shunning the pure and the impure.'
speaker: the deity of Kumano (as reported)
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Scroll number approximate.

paraphrase: At Saku in Shinano the dancing nenbutsu began: Ippen and his followers, beating time, danced as they recited in joy at their birth being settled; later performed on raised stages before great crowds.
speaker: narrator (Shōkai)
notes: Not in local corpus; recalled, no original quoted. Place and year as usually given; scroll number approximate.

paraphrase: Before dying Ippen burned the books he carried, saying that all the sacred teachings of his lifetime had come to an end in Namu Amida Butsu; he asked that no successor be set up and that his body be left in the fields for the beasts; he died reciting.

paraphrase: Myōe charges that the Senchakushū commits two great errors: it discards the aspiration for awakening (bodhicitta), which all the Pure Land sūtras, including the three grades of the Larger Sūtra, make the basis of birth; and it likens the practitioners of the holy path to the bandits of the two-rivers parable. The nenbutsu without the mind of awakening is not the Buddha's teaching.

paraphrase: Kōfukuji asks the court to stop Hōnen's exclusive nenbutsu for nine errors: establishing a new school without imperial sanction; making a new image (the maṇḍala of the embracing light that shows only nenbutsu people embraced); slighting Śākyamuni; hindering the myriad good practices; turning against the kami; being ignorant of the Pure Land (the grades of birth include other practices); misunderstanding the nenbutsu (reducing it to oral calling); harming the Buddhist order (despising precepts); and disturbing the nation.
